extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of English poetry / literary criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Lecture-style critical guidance on evaluating the poetry of Chaucer and Spenser, discussing qualities of description, tone, versification, allegory, and imagination with illustrative quotations and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gusto and local truth in natural description
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions of natural scenery should possess 'gusto' — a local truth and freshness that gives the very feeling of the air, the coolness or moisture of the ground; inanimate objects are made to have a fellow-feeling with the story's sentiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the opening of the Flower and the Leaf conveys coolness of the arbour, the starting up of birds, and the delight that rises with the song. Aim for sensory accuracy and a sense that nature reflects or responds to human feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trust in nature and simplicity of imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature should be the soul of art: a strength and simplicity in imagination that reposes entirely on nature and needs nothing else to supply it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chaucer's reliance on nature enables vivid portrayals (e.g., Griselda, Constance). Avoid affected rapture or flowery sentiment; let natural delight 'well out of the heart' like water from a spring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity of feeling — no affected rapture
rubrics_metrics.description: Emotional expression should be an unforced 'ebullition of natural delight,' not an affected or artificial rapture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text contrasts genuine emotional outpouring (Chaucer's nightingale passage) with 'flowery sentiment.' Anti-pattern: overwrought, manufactured feeling that lacks natural source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth of simple pathos and sustained sentiment
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry should sustain deep, simple pathos and intensity of conception without swerving from its subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chaucer's portrayals (e.g., Arcite's wasting sorrow) are cited as examples of sustained internal sentiment that 'never swerves from his subject.' Value continuity and psychological realism in depicting grief or heroism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mastery of tone: clear separation of comic and serious
rubrics_metrics.description: A skilled poet can pass 'from grave to gay, from lively to severe' while not confounding the two styles; when a piece is jest or earnest, the writer is exclusively taken up with it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chaucer handles both grave and comic styles well (Wife of Bath, Cock and the Fox). Anti-pattern: muddling comic elements with pathos except where nature mixes them unconsciously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vivid, picturesque imagery and painterly detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of vivid, painterly description — abrupt, rapid gleams that touch features and edges of a general mass — to create striking pictorial impressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spenser's Faery Queen abounds in such imagery (House of Pride, Bower of Bliss, Mask of Cupid). Example lines show combined sensory harmonies (birds, instruments, water). Beware making everything too literal when the effect sought is suggestive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of indefiniteness/suggestion to evoke abstractions
rubrics_metrics.description: To represent abstractions (Death, Night, Space) poetry often succeeds by leaving forms less definite and less bodily, approaching universality via suggestion rather than full physicalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with painting, which must render the visible. Example: Chaucer's three thieves searching for Death evoke the moral impression by suggestion; avoid over-embodying abstractions into mock-physical forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and richness in allegorical invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventiveness in subject-matter and allegorical personages — originality, richness, and variety — is a major merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spenser's allegorical figures (e.g., Procession of the Passions, Memory, Belphoebe, Florimel) show extraordinary originality. Reward imaginative novelty and a varied cast of allegorical types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allegory should not obstruct plain aesthetic appreciation
rubrics_metrics.description: Allegory need not prevent understanding or enjoyment; the poem should still be 'as plain as a pike-staff' to readers who ignore symbolic meanings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers can appreciate Spenser's stanzas and beauties (Britomart, Belphoebe) without decoding the allegory. Anti-pattern: allegory so obscure it 'bites' or obstructs immediate aesthetic pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between love of beauty and love of truth
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet's guiding principle (love of beauty vs. love of truth) affects work; excess devotion to beauty may detach the poet from truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spenser is characterized as guided by love of beauty, producing 'endless voluptuousness of sentiment' and fantasy. Value truthfulness where appropriate; excessive idealizing can make depiction less faithful to reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character portrayal: moral depth and fidelity
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters should be drawn with moral depth and fidelity to their nature; initial outlines that fix character simply and inimitably are praised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grisildis is given as an 'inimitable' first outline showing reverence, virtue, and steadfastness. Aim for character sketches that make moral qualities integral and convincing rather than merely illustrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Versification: strength, harmony, and attention to pronunciation
rubrics_metrics.description: Versification should have strength and harmony; apparent defects can arise from changes in pronunciation, and readers should sometimes restore historical pronunciations (e.g., pronounce final 'e').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The best general rule for reading Chaucer is to pronounce the final e, as in Italian, to regain rhythm. Scoring note: consider historical prosody when judging earliness of versification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of tone and ornament for subject (ceremony and grandeur)
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions of ceremonials, temples, and solemn rites should convey appropriate beauty and grandeur; careless modernizing or poor translation can lose the original feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temple descriptions in the Knight's Tale exemplify grandeur that Dryden's version loses. Ensure ornament and ritual imagery match the moral and emotional weight of the scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of linguistic liberties
rubrics_metrics.description: Occasional linguistic freedoms (archaisms, coinages) can be effective but may sometimes be unwarrantable or jar the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes some 'unwarrantable freedoms' Spenser took with language (e.g., odd word forms). Use inventive language judiciously; avoid obscuring sense or alienating readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic vigour: extravagance, licentiousness, and satire
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic humour may encompass extravagance and licentiousness rooted in the manners of the age; lively strokes of character and satire are valuable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chaucer and Boccaccio excel in both grave and comic styles: Wife of Bath's Prologue and Cock and the Fox are cited. Encourage vivacity, boldness, and satirical bite where appropriate, mindful of period context.
